lead: You feel you can't charge for something you haven't yet seen work with your own hands. The suspicion is reasonable, which is why a pep talk doesn't fix it. What fixes it is your own proof: do the service you sell a few times, record what happened, and book a conversation.
objetivo: replace the impostor feeling with your own proof: do the service you sell three times and book a conversation within 7 days.

aprende.t: See selling as getting the next step
Recognize the impostor cycle and its only way out
Do the service you sell before you defend it

hero_alt: A professional reviews printed pages of a diagnostic with a pen, with folders of previous cases beside them.

secoes.titulo: The impostor cycle and the way out
secoes.sub: The cycle feeds itself and never produces experience. Only one arrow leads out of it. Click each stage.

nos.detalhe: It's not a generic fear of failing. It's the suspicion, almost always correct, that you're promising a result without having your own track record with it.
One more tool, another niche, the presentation redone. Six months later your technical repertoire has doubled and your conversations with clients are still at zero.

Do you sell diagnostics? Diagnose three companies, even without charging. Do you sell review or teaching? Review three processes, teach three people. You don't need to believe it works: you need to have seen it work.
How long it took, what broke, where the person got stuck. This becomes your estimate and your answers to the hard questions.
No certificate will make the feeling of being ready appear. What exists is the first conversation on the calendar, and it works as a trigger.

secoes.legenda: Confidence in yourself doesn't come from conviction. It comes from your own historical data.

secoes.sub: Each one answers a common excuse.

texto: Selling, here, means getting another person to accept the next step with you: replying, booking the conversation, approving a small test.
You already do this every day, you just don't call it that. If you already sell without noticing, the problem isn't aptitude: it's method.

exemplo.texto: "If the service is good, it sells itself." A good service nobody knows about doesn't bring in revenue.

texto: You turn the car key without anxiety because it started the last hundred times. The confidence to say your price is built the same way: recorded repetition.
Counts: the same service in different contexts, with the time noted and another person using it. Doesn't count: redoing the test just for yourself or switching tools with every project.
"I need to do one more" can become a permanent excuse. The "being ready" line moves a little further ahead every time you get close.
The yardstick: keep going until you can show one complete thing from start to finish. From then on, service and conversation move together.

exemplo.texto: You have more versions of the presentation than conversations you've had.

texto: People who are already established also started without knowing how to price or where to find clients. They started and corrected along the way.
Swap "am I ready?" for "what's the smallest thing I can deliver well this week?" The second question has an answer, and it fits on a calendar.

secoes.sub: Run the prompt in the AI assistant you use. The plan is saved in a file with today's date.

blocos.conteudo:
You are my sales coach. I sell <the service: diagnosis, review,
advisory or teaching> to <type of company I want to serve>.

Here is everything I have already done or tested, unfiltered:
<one line per item, including unpaid work and tests that failed>

Do three things, in this order:
1. For each item, write the EVIDENCE in one sentence that I could say
   in a conversation with a client, without exaggerating and without making up numbers.
2. Point out the GAPS: what a buyer of this service would ask that I
   still can't answer from my own experience.
3. Propose 3 small things I can do in 7 days to close the
   most serious gaps, each with the observable result it would give me.

Be tough. If a piece of evidence is weak, say it's weak and explain why.

ANTI-IMPOSTOR PLAN · start <date>

Days 1 and 2 · pick ONE service and do it once
  - service: <diagnosis / review / teaching session>
  - case: <real or fictional company, but realistic>
  - if you don't finish in 2 days, the scope was too big: cut it in half

Days 3 and 4 · redo it in 2 other contexts (different industries)
  - time for each run: ___ / ___ / ___
  - what broke: ___

Day 5 · 3 outside people use or read it, with no explanation from you
  - where they got stuck: ___

Day 6 · proof inventory (prompt above), one sentence per piece of evidence

Day 7 · one scheduled conversation
  - with whom: ___   date and time: ___

secoes.sub: Do this week. The two together break the cycle with facts, not willpower.

exercicios.texto: List everything you've already done related to the service you want to sell and run the inventory prompt. Save the answer in a file with today's date.
exercicios.pronto: the file has at least 3 pieces of evidence, one sentence each, with no made-up numbers, and at least 2 uncomfortable gaps pointed out.

exercicios.texto: Fill in the anti-impostor plan. Before starting day 1, put the day 7 conversation on your calendar with someone you already know. The goal is not to sell: it's to talk about what you did with someone who isn't you.
exercicios.pronto: the day 7 conversation is on your calendar with name, date and time, and the service was done in 3 contexts with the time noted.

secoes.sub: 4 questions. The explanation appears after your attempt.

perguntas.p: You feel you can't charge for what you sell. What is the antidote in this lesson?
opcoes: Study one more tool until you feel confident
Do the service you sell a few times and record what happened
Lower the price until someone accepts
perguntas.explica: The impostor's suspicion is reasonable: you lack a track record of your own. Only proof fixes that. Studying more feels like progress, but it generates no data of your own.

perguntas.p: Which of these repetitions builds real confidence?
opcoes: Redoing the same test on your machine ten times
Doing the same diagnosis at three companies in different industries, noting the time
Watching someone do it and feeling like you learned
perguntas.explica: What counts is repetition in different contexts, with a record. Watching someone else do it leaves the track record with them, not with you.

perguntas.p: You keep putting off the first conversation because of a detail no client would ask about. What is happening?
opcoes: Preparation has become escape; set the date and show whatever is ready by then
A sign the service is not for you
perguntas.explica: The "being ready" line moves every time you get close. A fixed date stops it from moving.

perguntas.p: In the day 7 conversation, what is the goal?
opcoes: Talk about what you did with someone who isn't you
Present all the tools you've mastered
perguntas.explica: Day 7 exists so you sit in the chair. Selling comes later; the first conversation already breaks the cycle.

itens.texto: You already do this every day. What's missing is method, not aptitude.

itens.t: The block is a lack of proof
itens.texto: Talk doesn't fix it. Doing the work and recording it does.
Same service, different contexts, time noted.
Clarity is a result of acting. The scheduled conversation is the trigger.
